title: What is known about 1RB0LB_0RC0LE_1RD0RF_1LB1RB_0LA1RB_1RE---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LB_0RC0LE_1RD0RF_1LB1RB_0LA1RB_1RE---: it halts (Lean).
intro: This six-state machine is on the bbchallenge list of holdouts. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on. The headline: it halts from blank tape, proved in Lean.
verdict: It halts, proved in Lean (theorem halts_from_blank). The machine is a small rewriting system on the right half of its tape (the visit law, kernel-checked): blocks 000/100 are binary digits, blocks 1010 double the visits passing through, and a visit that meets 1011 halts. A checker for this system, proved correct in the kernel, finds that rounds 1 to 161,210 only rewrite and that round 161,211 meets 1011; that evaluation is by native_decide (compiled code), in ten segments. It halts after between 5.9 × 1024,266 and 9.2 × 1024,266 steps (computed, not proved).

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: The sweeps of the run
claims.text: The shift rules the machine uses in its run (every sweep met when the symbolic simulator runs from many configurations of the run), each for every number of copies.

claims.title: Both counters' increments, for all sizes
claims.text: One event (A on cell 3, phase 1) is the left increment (carry over n ones, digits 0110/0111) followed by the right increment in one pass: on a lowest 0 (18n+70 steps), over k+1 ones (6k+18n+76), across one junk unit (18n+110, 18n+116), across j units then k+1 ones (34j+6k+18n+82). 5 theorems.

claims.title: The visit law, in two forms
claims.text: A visit (the head on a 0 with a 0 on its left and a stream s on its right, in state C or F; it returns in state A two cells further left) rewrites the stream by 0 s → 1 s, 100 s → 000 v(s), 110 s → 000 v(s), 1010 s → 1010 v(v(s)), and halts the machine on 1011 s; for every stream and every left tape. Both forms obey the same rules. The run is a sequence of rounds 0^inf A> 1 0 0 S → 0^inf A> 1 0 0 v(1 0 S), starting after 6 steps with S = 1 0^inf.

claims.title: The abstract visit law and its count laws
claims.text: The four rules and the halting pattern as inductive relations on streams, with no machine in them; the 1010 rule is guarded (the stream behind must not start with 11), and after two visits a stream never starts with 11. Under n visits, 000 r and 100 r are binary digits that pass every second visit on, and 1010 r passes 2n visits on; likewise for "one of the first n visits halts".

claims.title: A checker for the visit law, proved correct
claims.text: scan carries a count of visits, kept as the pair e, c for 2e − c, through a finite word in one pass; hscan looks for a halting visit. Both are proved against the abstract system.

claims.title: If the checker accepts, the machine halts
claims.text: This machine satisfies the law, so for every k: if the checker runs k rounds from the word 1 and then finds a halting visit in the next round, the machine halts from blank tape. Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

claims.title: The machine halts from blank tape
claims.text: check 161210 [true] = true: rounds 1 to 161,210 use the four rewriting rules only, round 161,211 meets 1011. Evaluated with the checker compiled to native code, in ten segments chained by a kernel-checked lemma (about 3 hours of computing in all; the word grows to 1,001,253 cells). With the claim above: the machine halts. Besides the three standard axioms the theorem depends on eleven native_decide axioms, one per evaluation (trust in the Lean compiler). The number of steps is bounded separately (computed). Each segment was checked on 13 and 14 November 2026, and the whole check was run again from start to end on 14 November 2026 (HALT CHECKED). The repository's automatic checks cover the kernel-only part, not this evaluation.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 248 cells have been visited and 100 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: A direct run of 1011 steps (longrun.c, the simulator of tools/c/tm.h) without a halt.

claims.title: The left side is clockwork
claims.text: Between consecutive left-end extensions the busiest cell turns 3·2<sup>k</sup> times, each count twice (48, 96, 96, ..., 3·2<sup>22</sup>), in the first 1.5·10<sup>9</sup> steps.

claims.title: How much of the run the increments cover
claims.text: In the first 10<sup>8</sup> steps (513,702 events) 90.5% of the events are instances of these theorems (r0 256,841; r1 92,325; j10 75,989; j110 37,990; jk 1,733); the other 48,824 are carries over other junk layouts and the moments around the ends.

claims.title: The same round as the PR59 machines
claims.text: The three machines of busycoq PR59 (1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_0RD1RF_0RC--- and two relatives) obey the same law with one form of visit, and PR59 proves in Rocq that they halt in round 161,211. The proof here does not use PR59; our C simulator of the law (vis.c) also halts in that round on the PR59 machine. The twin 1RB0LB_0RC0LE_1RD0RF_1LB1RB_0LA0RE_1RE--- has its own theorem: machines with related tables are not claimed to halt together.

claims.title: Between 5.9 × 10<sup>24,266</sup> and 9.2 × 10<sup>24,266</sup> steps
claims.text: Computed, not proved: the machine halts after between 5.9 × 1024,266 and 9.2 × 1024,266 steps (178.4·280605 to 274.6·280605). Every visit costs a fixed number of steps of its own: 4 or 8 steps for 0 → 1 (entered in C or F), 6 for 100, 8 for 110, 20 for 1010. A C program repeats the checker's pass for all 161,210 rounds and adds up the visits per rule (5.9519·280605 of each main kind in the completed rounds, at most 2.1164·280605 more in the halting round). Its final word agrees cell for cell with the word the Lean segments check; the sums are in floating point, and the bounds are widened by 0.1% for that.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/exp
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.08). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.071).

claims.title: Two counters of the same events
claims.text: Read off the run: the counters on the two sides of the engine both go up by 1 at every visit of the head to the engine, one of them with fixed junk stretches between some digits; the junk is written when a carry reaches the end of the tape.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same tapes at another pace, whatever the states, as 1 other holdout (listed on the explainer page).

check: holdouts/1RB0LB_0RC0LE_1RD0RF_1LB1RB_0LA1RB_1RE---/lean/check_halt.sh   # the halting theorem: compiles the checker, then ten native_decide segments, about 3 hours

explainer.lede: Yes, it halts, and Lean has checked the proof. Behind two counters ticking together this machine is a small rewriting system: blocks 000/100 that act as binary digits, blocks 1010 that double the visits passing through, and a block 1011 that stops the machine. For 161,210 rounds the trap never forms; in round 161,211 it does. Nobody could watch that happen: it takes about 1024,266 steps.

facts.text: halts_from_blank, proved in Lean (kernel + native_decide for the checker run).
The machine as a rewriting system on streams; the checker and its correctness proof.
The first round in which a visit meets 1011.

sections.eyebrow: The whole machine in a few rules
sections.heading: The visit law
html: Forget the six states for a moment. Call everything from some cell to the right a stream. Whenever the head stands on a 0 with another 0 behind it and a stream in front, it wanders off into the stream and comes back out two cells further left, and the only thing that has changed is the stream. That excursion is a visit. What a visit does depends only on how the stream begins:

the stream beginsafter the visitLean
0 s1 sV_0
100 s000 then one visit to sV_100
110 s000 then one visit to sV_110
1010 s1010 then two visits to sV_1010
1011 sthe machine haltsV_1011_halts

So a block 000/100 is a binary digit: it flips on every visit and passes every second visit on. A block 1010 is a doubler: it passes every visit on twice. A block 1011 is a trap. The run from blank tape is a sequence of rounds: the tape is 0∞ A> 1 0 0 S, and one round puts 1 0 in front of the word S and makes one visit. Step through the first rounds:

These rules were first found for three sister machines, which busycoq PR59 proves to halt. This machine did not seem to fit: its visits start one cell further right, and they come in two forms, entered in state C or in state F. Running the table symbolically on every short beginning of a stream gives the rules for both forms, each as a Lean theorem that holds for every stream and every tape to the left.

In this machine the two forms behave identically: every rule in the table holds for a visit entered in C and for a visit entered in F (W_0, W_100, W_110, W_1010, W_1011_halts). Its twin is less tidy, which is why the abstract system below carries a small side condition that this machine never needs.

sections.heading: Counting visits instead of making them
html: After k rounds the word begins with about k/2 doublers, so about 2k/2 visits reach the blocks behind them. Nobody can replay that. But the visits to one block are all alike, so it is enough to carry their number through the word, block by block, in one pass:

• through a doubler 1010, n visits become 2n;
  • through a digit, n visits become n/2 (rounded up or down, depending on the digit), and the digit ends up as the parity of n;
  • a 0 where a block should start takes one visit to become a 1, and then the block behaves as above;
  • if a positive count reaches 1011, the machine halts.

The counts are huge but simple: each is a power of two minus a small number. Kept as a pair e, c standing for 2e − c, doubling is e+1 and halving is e−1, and every step of the pass is a few operations on small numbers. Pick a round and look at the counts:

The digits count the visits back down, so the count is small again at the right end of the word, where the word grows by a block now and then. For 161,210 rounds no pass ever meets 1011. In round 161,211 one does, in a word of 1,001,253 cells.

sections.heading: Three layers, each checked by Lean
html: The argument is a chain, and Lean's kernel checks every link except the last computation:

layerwhat it sayschecked by
1. The machine obeys the rulesFor every stream and every left tape, a visit in either form does what the table says, and a round is one visit (Visit.lean, generated from the transition table).kernel
2. The shortcuts are rightFor the rules as an abstract rewriting system, with no machine in it: n visits to a digit or a doubler do what the counting rules say (VisitLaw.lean).kernel
3. The program computes the shortcutsThe one-pass program scan returns exactly what the abstract system gives; so if the program reports a halting round, the machine halts (VisitCheck.lean, Law.lean).kernel
The run itselfThe program, run for 161,210 rounds, then finds the trap in the next round (VisitRun.lean).compiled code (native_decide)

The run is about 1011 list operations, too many for the kernel, so Lean compiles the program and trusts the outcome of the evaluation. It is cut into ten segments: each says "so many rounds take this word to that word", with the words at the boundaries (up to a million cells) written into the proof as numbers, and a small kernel-checked lemma chains the segments. Each segment takes 10 to 30 minutes and can be checked on its own.

The same round as three sister machines. The machines that busycoq PR59 proves to halt (in Rocq) obey the same law and halt in the same round, 161,211. The proof here does not use PR59, which makes the agreement a useful cross-check. The twin machine 1RB0LB_0RC0LE_1RD0RF_1LB1RB_0LA0RE_1RE--- has its own Lean theorem, proved from its own table; nothing is inferred from one machine to the other.

How many steps? Between 5.9 × 1024,266 and 9.2 × 1024,266: a number with about 24,267 digits, large but an ordinary power, not a power tower. Every visit costs a fixed number of the machine's own steps (4 or 8 steps for 0 → 1 (entered in C or F), 6 for 100, 8 for 110, 20 for 1010), so the step count is the number of visits times those costs, and the visits can be counted by the same one-pass shortcut: the largest count in round r is 2r/2, and over the whole run the visits of each main kind add up to about 6 to 8 times 280605. The two bounds differ because the last round stops part of the way through and because the two forms of visit cost slightly different amounts. This number is computed (by a program whose final tape agrees with the one Lean checks), not proved.

sections.heading: Two counters and an engine
html:
Most of the time the tape is L · engine · R. Each visit of the head to the engine is an event, and every event adds 1 to both counters. In the reference machine of the family (1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_0RD1RF_0RC---), L is written in blocks of four cells, 0101 for a 1 and 0001 for a 0, lowest digit next to the engine, and R keeps one cell per digit, three cells apart (the cells 9, 12, 15, … right of the head), lowest digit nearest the engine. Nine consecutive events of the reference machine right after its left-end visit at step 1,571,372 (the head in state A on the bold cell):

This machine is a relative in different clothes, the twin of 1RB0LB_0RC0LE_1RD0RF_1LB1RB_0LA0RE_1RE--- (E1 = 1RB against 0RE): the same clockwork left side (3·2k turns, each count twice, the second time 3 less) and the same tapes (at its left-end visit at step 12,788,128 its tape is exactly the twin's at step 14,008,454).

sections.heading: The left side is clockwork
html:
When L overflows, the carry runs to the left end of the tape, the tape grows by two cells there, and L starts again. The lowest digit of L is the cell where the head turns most often, and the number of its turns between two consecutive left-end extensions follows a strict pattern, without a single exception in the first 1.5·109 steps (ymax.c):

48 96 96 192 192 384 384 … 3·221 3·221 3·222

So the periods of the left side are powers of two in events, each length twice (the counter gains one digit every two periods). The time per event is not constant, because a carry on the right costs more when it crosses junk, so the steps between left-end extensions grow by factors between about 1.35 and 2.05 instead of exactly 2.

sections.heading: A counter with junk between its digits
html: The cells that change between events are the digits of the counters: each digit changes about half as often as the one before (chg.c counts, over a whole period, how often each cell changes from one event to the next). On the right, between some digits of R, there are stretches of fixed cells (0101010101 00 1 00 1 00 1 and the like) that the carries cross without changing. They are written when a carry runs into the end of the tape, at irregular event counts, and their layout is what makes the run irregular. How they are produced is not decoded yet.

sections.heading: The dangerous moments
html: The machine halts only in state F reading a 1, and F is entered from C1 (0RF) only. After C1, used about 3.1·107 times in 109 steps, the head has read a 0 every time (F0 is used exactly as often); no transition is rare. Halting would need that ordinary step to find a 1. In every run short enough to simulate directly this has not happened. The proof above shows that it does happen, in round 161,211.

sections.heading: Eight machines, one mechanism
html: The family (G11-Y): 1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_0RD1RF_0RC--- (the reference), 1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_0RD1RB_0RC--- (the same run), 1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_0RD0LC_0RC---, 1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_1RB0RD_0RB---, 1RB0LB_0RC0LF_1LD1RE_0LA0RB_0RD0RF_0LA--- (all with left-end extensions after 2k events, each twice, to within a few hundred steps of each other); 1RB0LB_0RC0LE_1RD0RF_1LB1RB_0LA0RE_1RE--- and 1RB0LB_0RC0LE_1RD0RF_1LB1RB_0LA1RB_1RE--- (the same right part, a differently written left counter); and the mirror case 1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RB_0RD1RF_1LA---, with the junk on the left.

sections.heading: The increments, proved for every size
html: As in its twin, the tape holds the reference's two counters in other words; here one visit to the engine (A on cell 3) does the left increment and then the right one in a single pass. lean/Events.lean proves the combined visit for every size.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.08). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.071).
After 109 steps the tape spans 248 cells (88 left of the start, 152 right), with a density of 1s of 0.403.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same tapes at another pace (observed, not proved). Leave the states aside and compare only the tape and the place of the head. Then a large part of the first 107 configurations of this machine are configurations of the machines below, in the same order and up to the end of the run. The steps at which they occur differ, the tables are not renamings of each other, and equal tapes with different states may be continued differently, so this does not tie the halting questions together.

summary: Halts (Lean, with native_decide for the evaluation of a verified checker): a rewriting system on streams (visit law, kernel-checked) whose round 161,211 meets the halting block 1011; the same law and round as the busycoq PR59 machines, proved here independently.
